title: Forces and their effects
subtitle: Contact and non-contact forces, vector diagrams, moments and the principle of moments
lede: Everything in Topic 9, split into two bands. The non-negotiables are the kinds of force, interaction pairs, vectors, free body diagrams, resultant forces, moments and the principle of moments, levers and gears, and lubrication. The tricky bits are where the marks go missing: scale drawings and resolving, equilibrium, explaining motion, moments with a twist, levers as force multipliers, and the hand-winch 6-marker on gears, force and work. Sections marked P are Physics only (not Combined Science); H is Higher tier only.
howto: Start with the non-negotiables. Do not move on from a section until every practice question is green.
Draw every free body diagram and scale drawing yourself on paper — ruler, protractor, stated scale — before you look at the one on the page.
Read each explanation, then cover it and say it back. For a definition, the bold words are the ones the mark is for.
Do the practice questions before opening the hint or walkthrough. Calculations in EWAU layout on paper first, then type the answer to check it.
For "explain" and "describe how" questions, write your answer in full sentences, then compare it with the model answer line by line.
Fill in the traffic-light self-check at the end of each section. Anything red or amber is what to revise next.

sections.title: Contact and non-contact forces
equations: \text{contact: normal contact force, friction, tension, drag, upthrust}

parts.title: The two kinds
parts.html:
Non-contact forcesFieldExample
Gravitational (weight)gravitational field — a region where a mass experiences a forcethe Earth pulls an apple down; the Sun holds the planets
Electrostaticelectric field — a region where a charge experiences a forcea charged balloon lifts hair; like charges repel
Magneticmagnetic field — a region where a magnetic material (or another magnet, or a current) experiences a forcea magnet lifts a paperclip; two north poles repel
Contact forcesWhat it isExample
Normal contact force (reaction)a surface pushing back on whatever presses on it, always at right angles (normal) to the surfacethe table holding up a book
Frictionthe force between two surfaces that opposes their sliding; it transfers energy to the thermal storebrakes; shoes gripping the floor
Tensionthe pull along a stretched rope, string or cablea crane cable
Drag (air resistance, water resistance)friction with a fluid, opposing motion through ita parachute
Upthrustthe upward push of a fluid on an object in ita boat floating

The June 2024 scheme (Q1(b)) credited "a region where a charge experiences a force" for an electric field; the same shape of sentence does for the other two fields. The June 2023 report (Q5(b), a magnet floating above another): "many answers had the words magnetic fields but usually in terms of repelling" — say that the fields interact to produce the force, then that the repulsion balances the weight. The June 2023 scheme (Q4(a)(iv)) and June 2024 scheme (Q4(a)) — both for the force a fluid exerts on a surface — gave the mark for an arrow normal to the surface at the point and required it to touch the point (or the dot) where it acts; draw a normal contact force the same way.

parts.title: Naming the forces
parts.question: A magnet is held above a second magnet so that it floats. Describe the forces acting on the upper magnet. Use the idea of magnetic fields in your answer. (3 marks)
steps: The magnetic fields of the two magnets interact (like poles facing), producing a repulsive force upwards on the upper magnet — a non-contact force.
The Earth's gravitational field pulls the upper magnet down: its weight, also non-contact.
The repulsion is equal in size and opposite to the weight, so the resultant force is zero and the magnet stays at rest.

questions.text: Which of these is a non-contact force?
questions.explain: Weight is the gravitational force — it acts through the gravitational field without touching.

questions.text: A book rests on a table. Name the two forces acting on the book and state whether each is a contact or non-contact force. (2)
questions.model:
• Its weight (gravitational force, downwards) — non-contact.
  • The normal contact force from the table (upwards) — contact.

questions.text: State what is meant by a gravitational field. (1)
questions.model: • A region in which a mass experiences a force.

questions.text: Two charged balloons push each other apart. Which field is responsible?
questions.explain: Charges interact through electric fields.

questions.text: A box is pushed along a floor at constant speed. Name the contact force that opposes the motion and describe what it does to the energy of the box. (2)
questions.model:
• Friction between the box and the floor.
  • It transfers energy from the box's kinetic store to the thermal store of the surfaces (they warm up), so the push is needed just to keep the speed constant.

questions.text: A block rests on a slope. Describe the direction of the normal contact force on the block. (1)
questions.model: • At right angles to the surface of the slope (not vertically upwards), pushing away from the slope.

checklist: Give examples of forces that act at a distance and name the field responsible
Give examples of contact forces, including normal contact force and friction
Describe what a field is
sections.blurb: Every force is one object acting on another. Some need the objects to touch; some act across a gap through a field. Naming the right force, and the field behind it, is the first mark in most Paper 2 force questions.

sections.title: Interaction pairs: forces come in twos

parts.title: Pairs and how to spot them
parts.html:
An interaction pair (Newton's third law pair) is two forces that are equal in size, opposite in direction, of the same type (both gravitational, or both contact…), and act on different objects. Written as a sentence: "the Earth pulls the book down with 5 N; the book pulls the Earth up with 5 N". Swap the two nouns and the force is its partner. In the exam name both forces with both objects: June 2025 1H Q8(a)(iii) gave a mark for "equal and opposite", a mark for "the force exerted by the foot on the ball" and a mark for "the force exerted by the ball on the foot"; "action and reaction" on its own is capped at 1 mark and an answer in terms of energy scores nothing (June 2022 1H Q7(c)(ii)).

The weight of the book and the normal contact force from the table are not a pair: they act on the same object (the book) and are different types (gravity and contact). They happen to be equal because the book is in equilibrium; tip the table and they are no longer equal, while the real pairs stay equal always.

Both forces of a pair are vectors — they can be drawn as arrows of the same length pointing opposite ways, one on each object (9.1c).

parts.title: The pair to the weight
parts.question: A student says: "The weight of a cup on a table and the normal contact force from the table are an interaction pair because they are equal and opposite." Explain why the student is wrong and identify the correct partner force to the cup's weight. (3 marks)
steps: The two forces the student names both act on the same object (the cup) and are different types (gravitational and contact), so they cannot be an interaction pair — pairs act on different objects and are the same type.
They are equal only because the cup is in equilibrium (balanced forces), not because they are a pair.
The partner to the weight (the Earth pulling the cup down) is the cup pulling the Earth up with an equal gravitational force.

questions.text: State the four features of an interaction pair of forces. (2)
questions.model:
• Equal in size and opposite in direction…
  • …of the same type, acting on different objects. (Two features per mark.)

questions.text: A footballer kicks a ball with a force of 200 N. What is the partner force?
options: The ball pushing on the boot with 200 N
The ground pushing up on the footballer
questions.explain: Swap the nouns: boot on ball ↔ ball on boot, same size, opposite direction.

questions.text: A rocket pushes exhaust gas downwards. Identify the partner force and explain how it makes the rocket accelerate upwards. (2)
questions.model:
• The rocket exerts a force on the gas (downwards); the gas exerts an equal and opposite force on the rocket (upwards) — name both forces with both objects.
  • If that upward force is larger than the rocket's weight there is a resultant upward force, so it accelerates upwards.

questions.text: A book rests on a table. Which pair of forces is an interaction pair?
options: The book's weight and the normal contact force on the book
The normal contact force on the book and the book's push on the table
The table's weight and the book's weight
questions.explain: Table pushes book up / book pushes table down: same type (contact), different objects.

questions.text: A swimmer pushes backwards on the water with her hands. Explain how this moves her forwards. (2)
questions.model:
• Her hands exert a force on the water (backwards); the water exerts an equal and opposite force on her hands (forwards) — the interaction pair, both forces named with both objects.
  • This forward force on the swimmer is greater than the drag, giving a resultant force forwards, so she accelerates.

questions.text: An apple of weight 1 N hangs from a tree. State the size and direction of the gravitational force the apple exerts on the Earth. (1)
questions.model: • 1 N, upwards (towards the apple) on the Earth.

checklist: State the four properties of an interaction pair
Identify both forces of a pair in a situation
Distinguish an interaction pair from balanced forces on one object
sections.blurb: Whenever two objects interact, each exerts a force on the other: equal in size, opposite in direction, the same type, one on each object. These pairs are not the same thing as two balanced forces on one object — the exam trap of the topic.

sections.title: Vectors and scalars

parts.title: The lists and the arrow
parts.html:
Vectors (size and direction)Scalars (size only)
force, weight, velocity, displacement, acceleration, momentumspeed, distance, mass, energy, work done, power, time, temperature, density, pressure*

*Pressure acts in all directions at a point, so it is a scalar; the force it produces on a surface is a vector.

A vector is drawn as an arrow: the length shows the size (to a stated scale) and the arrowhead shows the direction. Two vectors are only equal if both size and direction match — which is why a car going round a bend at a steady 30 mph has a constant speed but a changing velocity (Topic 2).

Explain-the-difference questions want an example pair: "speed is a scalar — 5 m/s; velocity is a vector — 5 m/s north", or "mass is a scalar — 2 kg; weight is a vector — 20 N downwards".

parts.title: The 2-mark explanation
parts.question: Explain the difference between a vector quantity and a scalar quantity, giving an example of each. (2 marks)
steps: A vector has both a size (magnitude) and a direction; a scalar has size only.
Example: force (10 N to the left) is a vector; mass (2 kg) is a scalar. Any correct pair scores.

questions.text: Which row is all vectors?
questions.explain: Speed, mass, time, energy, distance and temperature are scalars.

questions.text: State what is meant by a vector quantity. (1)
questions.model: • A quantity that has both size (magnitude) and direction.

questions.text: Which quantity is a scalar?
questions.explain: Work done (energy transferred) has no direction.

questions.text: A diagram shows a force as an arrow. State what the length and the direction of the arrow represent. (2)
questions.model:
• The length represents the size of the force (to a scale).
  • The direction of the arrow is the direction of the force.

questions.text: Two forces of 6 N act on an object. Explain why the resultant force could be anything from 0 N to 12 N. (2)
questions.model:
• Force is a vector, so the resultant depends on the directions as well as the sizes.
  • In the same direction they add to 12 N; in opposite directions they cancel to 0 N; at an angle, somewhere between.

questions.text: A car travels at a steady 20 m/s round a roundabout. Which statement is correct?
options: Its speed and velocity are both constant
Its speed is constant but its velocity changes because its direction changes
Its velocity is constant but its speed changes
questions.explain: Velocity is a vector: changing direction is a changing velocity.

checklist: Define vector and scalar quantities
Sort force, velocity, displacement, acceleration, momentum, speed, distance, mass, energy, time, temperature
Explain how an arrow represents a vector
sections.blurb: A vector has a size and a direction; a scalar has size only. Force is a vector, which is why it is drawn as an arrow and why two forces can add to less than their sum.

sections.title: Free body force diagrams
equations: \text{one object, arrows from its centre, labelled, to scale}

parts.title: The rules
parts.html:
1. One object only. Draw it as a box or a dot; leave out the table, the ground, the rope — only the forces they exert on the object appear.
  2. Every arrow starts at the centre of the object (or its line passes through the centre). On a picture of the situation a force is drawn where it acts — a contact force at the point of contact (N1); on a free body diagram the object is a box or a dot and every force is drawn from its centre. The June 2025 report (Q8(b)(iii)): "examiners were looking for correctly labelled vectors that would both pass through the centre of the block"; arrows near the edges were penalised because the block would spin.
  3. Direction: weight straight down; normal contact force at right angles to the surface; friction and drag against the motion; tension along the rope.
  4. Label each arrow with the force's name and size. "Force vectors must have a size as well as a direction" — unlabelled arrows scored 1 of 2.
  5. Lengths in proportion: equal forces, equal arrows; a 10 N arrow twice as long as a 5 N one.

Reading one: if the arrows balance (equal and opposite in every direction) the resultant is zero and the object is at rest or moving at constant velocity; a longer arrow one way means a resultant that way and an acceleration that way (N5).

parts.title: Three situations
parts.question: Describe the free body diagrams for (a) a book at rest on a table, (b) a car moving at constant velocity along a flat road, (c) a skydiver just after jumping. (3 marks)
steps: (a) Two arrows from the centre: weight down and normal contact force up, equal lengths.
(b) Four arrows: weight down and normal contact force up, equal; driving force forwards and drag + friction backwards, equal — constant velocity means zero resultant.
(c) Weight down, long; air resistance up, short — the resultant is downwards, so the skydiver accelerates downwards.

questions.text: A 5 N block rests on a table. Describe the free body diagram for the block. (2)
questions.model:
• A 5 N weight arrow straight down from the centre, and a 5 N normal contact force arrow straight up through the centre.
  • The two arrows are the same length and both labelled with 5 N.

questions.text: A student draws the weight arrow of a block starting at its bottom-left corner. Why does this lose a mark?
options: Force arrows must pass through the centre of the object — drawn at a corner, the force would make the block rotate
questions.explain: The 2025 report's exact point.

questions.text: A sledge is pulled along flat snow by a rope at constant speed. Name the four forces on the sledge's free body diagram and state which pairs are equal. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1VerticalWeight down and normal contact force up — equal.
2HorizontalTension in the rope forwards and friction (between runners and snow) backwards, opposing the motion; they are equal, so there is no resultant force and the sledge moves at constant velocity. The vertical forces are balanced too (it does not move up or down) and do not affect the horizontal motion (Nov 2020 2H Q9(c)).
3DrawingAll four from the centre, labelled, equal pairs the same length.

questions.text: A free body diagram of a car shows a 2000 N driving force forwards and 1500 N of drag backwards. What is the resultant force?
questions.explain: $2000 - 1500 = 500$ N in the direction of the larger force.

questions.text: Explain what the free body diagram of a ball thrown upwards looks like at the top of its flight (ignore air resistance). (2)
questions.model:
• One arrow only: the weight, straight down from the centre.
  • There is no upward force — the hand stopped pushing when the ball left it; the weight gives a downward resultant, so the ball accelerates downwards even while momentarily at rest.

questions.text: A block hangs at rest from a string. State the two forces on the block, their directions and how their sizes compare. (2)
questions.model:
• Weight downwards and tension in the string upwards.
  • They are equal in size (the block is at rest, so the resultant is zero).

checklist: Draw a free body diagram for an object at rest, moving steadily, and accelerating
Label each arrow with the name and size of the force
Read the resultant force off a free body diagram
sections.blurb: A free body diagram shows all the forces on one object and nothing else. The marks are for arrows that start at (or point through) the centre, point the right way, are labelled with their sizes, and have lengths in proportion.

sections.title: Resultant force along a line, and balanced forces

parts.title: Resultant and what it does
parts.html:
The resultant force is one force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together. Along a line: forces in the same direction add; forces in opposite directions subtract, and the resultant is in the direction of the larger. 700 N forwards and 400 N backwards → 300 N forwards.

ResultantMotionName
zeroat rest, or moving at constant velocity (steady speed in a straight line)balanced forces, equilibrium
not zeroaccelerates in the direction of the resultant: speeds up, slows down or changes direction ($F = m \times a$, Topic 2)unbalanced forces

Two traps. "Balanced forces" is not the same as "no forces": a car at 70 mph on the motorway has four forces on it, all balanced. And a zero resultant does not mean the object is stationary — a parachutist at terminal velocity has balanced forces and is falling fast.

The spec's phrase (9.5): an isolated object or system — treat the object (or a group of objects moving together, like a car and its trailer) as one thing and add up only the external forces on it; forces between the parts of the system cancel in pairs.

parts.title: A tug of war
parts.question: Team A pulls a rope with 1500 N to the left; team B pulls with 1200 N to the right. (a) Calculate the resultant force on the rope. (b) Describe the motion of the rope. (c) Later the teams pull with equal forces. State the resultant and describe the motion. (4 marks)
steps: (a) Opposite directions, so subtract: $1500 - 1200 = 300$ N to the left (the direction of the larger force).
(b) There is a resultant force, so the rope accelerates to the left — it starts moving, speeding up towards team A.
(c) Resultant zero. The forces are balanced: the rope stays at rest if it was at rest, or keeps moving at a constant velocity if it was already moving — it does not have to stop.

questions.text: A boat's engine pushes it forwards with 3000 N; water resistance is 1800 N. Calculate the size and direction of the resultant force.
walkthrough: $3000 - 1800 = 1200$ N forwards — the direction is a separate mark (June 2018 2H Q7(a)(i): \"0.9 (kN) (1) upwards (1)\").

questions.text: The resultant force on a moving object is zero. Which must be true?
options: It moves at constant velocity (or is at rest)
questions.explain: Zero resultant → velocity does not change.

questions.text: Two people push a car in the same direction with 250 N and 300 N; friction is 400 N. Calculate the size and direction of the resultant force.
questions.hint: Add the two pushes, subtract the friction.
walkthrough: $250 + 300 = 550$ N forwards; $550 - 400 = 150$ N forwards (state the direction — it is a mark).

questions.text: A skydiver falls at a constant speed of 50 m/s. A student says the forces on him must be unbalanced because he is moving so fast. Explain why the student is wrong. (2)
questions.model:
• Constant speed in a straight line means the velocity is not changing, so there is no acceleration.
  • No acceleration means the resultant force is zero: air resistance equals his weight. Speed itself does not need a resultant force.

questions.text: A lift accelerates upwards. Compare the tension in its cable with the weight of the lift and explain your answer. (2)
questions.model:
• The tension is greater than the weight.
  • An acceleration upwards needs a resultant force upwards, so the upward force (tension) must exceed the downward force (weight).

questions.text: A car and its trailer are treated as one system. Which force is NOT counted when finding the resultant force on the system?
options: The driving force on the car's tyres
The pull of the car on the trailer through the tow bar
questions.explain: The tow-bar forces are internal to the system and cancel as an interaction pair.

checklist: Calculate the resultant of forces along a line and state its direction
State what a zero resultant means for the motion
Link the direction of the resultant to the direction of the acceleration
sections.blurb: The resultant force is the single force that would have the same effect as all the forces together. Along a line it is add-and-subtract. Zero resultant does not mean 'stopped' — it means the velocity is not changing.

sections.title: Moment of a force: the turning effect

parts.title: Moments
parts.html:
Situations with rotation (9.6P): a door on its hinges, a spanner on a nut, a see-saw, a wheelbarrow, a crowbar, a bicycle pedal, a steering wheel, scissors, a tap. In each there is a pivot (hinge, nut, fulcrum, axle) and a force applied some distance from it.

Moment of a force (9.7P) $= $ force $\times$ distance normal to the direction of the force (the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line of action). Unit: newton metre, N m (the June 2024 scheme's one-mark question). It is not a joule even though both are $\text{N} \times \text{m}$: in a moment the distance is across the force, in work it is along it.

Why perpendicular: only the part of the force at right angles to the lever turns it. Pushing straight along a spanner towards the nut does nothing; pushing at right angles at the far end does the most. So: bigger force or longer perpendicular distance → bigger moment. That is why door handles are far from the hinges and why a long spanner loosens a stiff nut.

Units trap (June 2022 report, Q6): "the most common detracting mistake was not converting cm to m" — a 30 cm spanner is 0.30 m, or the moment comes out 100 times too big.

parts.title: A door
parts.question: A door handle is 0.80 m from the hinges. A person pushes the handle with a force of 15 N at right angles to the door. (a) Calculate the moment. (b) Explain why pushing with the same force 0.20 m from the hinges is much harder to open the door with.
steps: Equation: $M = F \times d$
Working: $M = 15 \times 0.80$
Answer: $= 12$
Units: N m
(b) At 0.20 m the moment is only $15 \times 0.20 = 3$ N m — a quarter of the turning effect for the same force, so four times the force would be needed for the same moment.

questions.text: A spanner is 25 cm long. A mechanic pushes on its end with 60 N at right angles. Calculate the moment about the nut.
What is the unit of the moment of a force?
questions.explain: Newton metre. Not the joule, even though $J = N m$ dimensionally, because the distance is perpendicular to the force, not along it.

questions.text: A moment of 24 N m is needed to turn a stiff tap. The tap handle is 0.08 m long. Calculate the force needed at its end.
walkthrough: $F = \dfrac{M}{d} = \dfrac{24}{0.08} = 300$ N. (Divide: the June 2022 2H scheme (Q6(b)(i)) rejected $0.6 \times 3$ for a force from a moment of 0.60 N m at 3 cm — and the cm had to become 0.03 m.)

questions.text: Explain why it is easier to loosen a wheel nut with a long wheel brace than with a short one. (2)
questions.model:
• Moment = force × perpendicular distance; the long brace puts the hand at a greater distance from the nut.
  • So the same force produces a bigger moment — or the moment needed to loosen the nut is produced with a smaller force.

questions.text: A force of 10 N acts on a lever 0.5 m from the pivot, but at 30° to the lever instead of at right angles. The moment is…
questions.explain: The perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force is less than 0.5 m, so the moment is less than 10 × 0.5.

questions.text: State what is meant by the moment of a force. (2)
questions.model:
• The turning effect of a force about a pivot.
  • Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force (N m).

checklist: Describe situations where a force causes rotation
Use moment = force × distance normal to the direction of the force
Use the unit N m, and explain why d must be the perpendicular distance
sections.blurb: A force on something that can pivot makes it turn. The size of the turning effect is the moment: force × the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force. Longer spanner, bigger moment.

sections.title: The principle of moments

parts.title: The principle and how it is marked
parts.html:
The principle of moments: for an object in equilibrium (balanced, not rotating), the sum of the clockwise moments about a pivot equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about the same pivot.

The June 2024 scheme (Q6(b)(i), 2 marks) gave one mark for "sum of the clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments (about the same point)" and a separate mark for "for a system in equilibrium". The June 2022 report: "just saying clockwise moments = anticlockwise moments would not score" — when the question says state the principle, the totals ("sum of" or "total") and in equilibrium are the two marks (June 2022 Q6(b)(iii), June 2024 Q6(b)(i)). Asked only for the relationship between two moments, Nov 2021 Q6(a) accepted "the moments are equal". In a calculation, masses in grams can be used directly — $g$ cancels from every term (June 2018 2H Q6(b)).

Calculations: decide which side turns which way, write each moment as force × distance, set the totals equal, solve. The June 2023 report: "questions asking for the principle of moments will expect you to show a calculation of moments using force × distance" — students who used ratios of forces and distances without calculating a moment lost marks, even with the right answer. Keep the distances all in m (or all in cm — consistent units were accepted) and measure every distance from the pivot, not from the end of the beam.

parts.title: An unknown distance
parts.question: A uniform beam is pivoted at its centre. A 200 N box sits 1.5 m to the left of the pivot. Calculate how far to the right of the pivot a 300 N box must be placed to balance the beam.
steps: Anticlockwise moment (left box) $= 200 \times 1.5 = 300$ N m.
Clockwise moment (right box) $= 300 \times d$.
In equilibrium, sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments: $300 \times d = 300$, so $d = 1.0$ m.

questions.text: State the principle of moments. (2)
questions.model:
• The sum of the clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point…
  • …when the object is in equilibrium (balanced).

questions.text: A see-saw is pivoted at its centre. A 450 N child sits 1.2 m from the pivot. Calculate the force needed 1.8 m from the pivot on the other side to balance it.
walkthrough: Sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments (in equilibrium); moment = force × distance — both lines carry marks (June 2018 2H Q6(b)).

questions.text: A metre rule balances on a pivot at its centre. A 4 N weight hangs 20 cm left of the pivot. Calculate how far right of the pivot a 5 N weight must hang.
A student answers a principle-of-moments question by writing "$300 \div 200 = 1.5$, so the distance is $1.5 \times 1 = 1.5$ m" and gets the right number. Why might this lose marks?
options: No moment was calculated as force × distance, which is what the question asks to be shown
Ratios are not allowed in physics
questions.explain: The 2023 report's exact point: show the moments.

questions.text: A uniform plank is pivoted at its centre. A 60 N weight hangs 0.5 m to the left and a 20 N weight hangs 1.0 m to the left. A single weight W hangs 1.6 m to the right.
Explain why a person can lift a heavy load in a wheelbarrow with a force much smaller than the load's weight. (2)
questions.model:
• The wheel is the pivot; the load is close to it and the handles are far from it.
  • By the principle of moments, effort × long distance = load × short distance, so the effort is smaller than the load by the ratio of the distances.

checklist: State the principle of moments in full
Use it to find an unknown force or distance
Show the working the examiners expect: both moments calculated as force × distance
sections.blurb: If something pivoted is balanced — not turning — the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment about the pivot. Say 'sum of', say 'in equilibrium', and show the moment calculations.

sections.title: Levers and gears: passing a turning effect on

parts.title: Levers
parts.html: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a pivot. The effort is the force you apply; the load is the force the lever applies to the thing being moved. By the principle of moments, just as it starts to move: effort × distance of effort from pivot = load × distance of load from pivot. Put the effort far from the pivot and the load near it and the lever is a force multiplier: the crowbar above turns 100 N into 600 N. The price is distance — the effort end moves six times as far as the load end (see Levers: force multipliers in the tricky bits).

parts.title: Gears
parts.html:
Two gears mesh tooth to tooth. The force one tooth pushes on the other with is the same on both wheels (an interaction pair), but it acts at each wheel's own radius, so the moment on each wheel is proportional to its radius (and so to its number of teeth).

  • Small driving large: the large wheel gets a bigger moment but turns fewer times (slower) — a force multiplier, used for climbing hills on a bike, in a winch, in a car's low gear.
  • Large driving small: the small wheel gets a smaller moment but turns more times (faster) — a speed multiplier, a bike's top gear.
  • Meshed gears turn in opposite directions; a chain or belt between two wheels keeps them turning the same way.
  • Turns × teeth is the same for both wheels (turns of A : turns of B = teeth of B : teeth of A): a 10-tooth wheel must turn twice to turn a 20-tooth wheel once, because the same number of teeth pass the contact point on each.

The June 2024 scheme (Q6(c)): a gear with three times the teeth turns at a third of the rate; to make an output turn twice as fast, add a wheel with half the teeth meshing with it.

parts.title: A bicycle
parts.question: A cyclist's pedal wheel has 48 teeth and drives, through a chain, a rear wheel gear with 16 teeth. (a) How many times does the rear gear turn for one turn of the pedals? (b) Compare the moment on the rear gear with the moment on the pedal wheel. (c) Explain why the cyclist changes to a 32-tooth rear gear for a hill. (4 marks)
steps: (a) The chain moves the same distance round both wheels, so turns × teeth is the same for both (or gear ratio $48:16 = 3:1$ — June 2019 2H Q4(c)(i)): $48 \div 16 = 3$ turns of the rear gear per pedal turn.
(b) The chain pulls both wheels with the same force; the rear gear has one third of the radius, so it gets one third of the moment — a speed multiplier.

(c) With 32 teeth the rear gear's radius is larger, so the same chain force gives a bigger moment on the wheel — more turning force to climb — while the wheel turns only 1.5 times per pedal turn, so the bike goes slower.

questions.text: A crowbar has its pivot 0.1 m from a rock and the effort is applied 0.9 m from the pivot. The rock needs a force of 450 N to move. Calculate the effort needed.
A 12-tooth gear drives a 36-tooth gear. For one turn of the 36-tooth gear, the 12-tooth gear turns…
questions.explain: 36 teeth must pass the contact point; the small wheel has 12, so three turns.

questions.text: Explain how a small gear driving a larger gear increases the turning effect. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1Same forceThe force between the meshing teeth is the same on both gears.
2Bigger radiusOn the larger gear that force acts at a greater distance from the axle (larger radius).
3MomentMoment = force × distance, so the larger gear has the greater moment (it turns more slowly in exchange).

questions.text: Two meshed gears: A turns clockwise. B turns…
questions.explain: Meshed gears turn opposite ways.

questions.text: A motor turns a 40-tooth gear at 60 turns per minute. Describe how to add a gear so that an output turns at 120 turns per minute, and explain your choice. (2)
questions.model:
• Add a gear meshing with the 40-tooth gear only (next to it, touching no other), with 20 teeth (half as many) — the June 2024 2H scheme (Q6(c)(ii)) gave one mark for linking it to the named wheel and one for the tooth count.
  • The same number of teeth pass the contact point on each, so the 20-tooth gear makes two turns for every one of the 40-tooth gear: 120 per minute.

questions.text: Explain why a lever with the effort far from the pivot and the load near it is called a force multiplier, and what the user gives up in return. (2)
questions.model:
• Effort × its distance = load × its distance, so with a longer effort distance the load force is larger than the effort.
  • The effort has to move further than the load does (the work done is the same, ignoring friction).

sections.title: Lubrication: reducing unwanted energy transfer

parts.title: Friction, lubrication and the 'how' mark
parts.html:
When two surfaces slide over each other, friction acts and work is done against it; the energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surfaces and the air — it heats them up and spreads out (dissipates), so it is no longer useful. In a machine that lowers the efficiency (Topic 3): more of the input energy ends up as heat and less as useful output.

A lubricant (oil, grease, graphite) is a thin layer that separates the surfaces so they slide on the fluid instead of rubbing directly; the frictional force is smaller, so less work is done against friction, less energy is dissipated as heat, and more is transferred usefully.

Where friction is wanted — brakes, tyres, shoes, a match — you do not lubricate; you increase the grip (rougher surface, larger normal force).

The June 2025 report (Q2(a)(iii)): asked for one way to reduce the gap between a trolley's measured and predicted speed down a runway, "many candidates answered in general terms of reducing friction rather than how this could be achieved" — "reduce friction" scored nothing; "oil the wheel axles" scored (the scheme also accepted an air track, a steeper runway and streamlining the trolley). The June 2023 report said the same for practical improvements: "you need to say how it will improve, not why".

parts.title: Say how
parts.question: A pupil's trolley rolls more slowly down a ramp than the calculation predicts. (a) Explain why. (b) Suggest one way to reduce the difference. (3 marks)
steps: (a) Friction at the axles and bearings (and air resistance) does work against the motion, transferring some of the trolley's energy to the thermal store instead of its kinetic store — so it ends up slower than predicted.
(b) Lubricate the axles with oil (a method)…
…which separates the moving surfaces, reducing the frictional force and the energy dissipated. ("Reduce friction" alone is a reason, not a method, and scores nothing.)

questions.text: Explain how lubricating the moving parts of a machine increases its efficiency. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1FrictionWithout lubricant the surfaces rub; work is done against friction and energy is transferred to the thermal store (dissipated / wasted).
2LubricantThe oil reduces friction, so less energy is transferred to the thermal store (less is wasted).
3EfficiencyMore useful energy is available for the same input (or less input energy is needed for the same useful output), and $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{useful energy transferred}}{\text{total energy supplied}}$ — stating the equation is the third mark (June 2019 2H Q4(c)(ii)).

questions.text: A trolley runs down a runway more slowly than the calculation predicts. A question asks: "Suggest one way to reduce the difference." Which answer scores?
questions.explain: A method, not a reason.

questions.text: Describe what happens to the energy when work is done against friction. (2)
questions.model:
• It is transferred to the thermal store of the surfaces and surroundings (they get warmer).
  • It spreads out / dissipates and is no longer useful.

questions.text: Where should friction NOT be reduced?
options: The brake pads of a car
questions.explain: Brakes work by friction.

questions.text: A bicycle chain squeaks and the cyclist has to pedal harder. Explain what has happened and what to do. (2)
questions.model:
• The chain has lost its lubricant, so there is more friction between the links and the gear teeth; more of the pedalling energy is transferred to the thermal store (dissipated) — the June 2024 2H scheme (Q7(b)(iii)) ignores "sound".
  • Oil the chain: the oil separates the metal surfaces and reduces the frictional force.

checklist: Explain how friction wastes energy in a machine
Explain how lubrication reduces the waste

sections.blurb: Friction between moving parts transfers energy to the thermal store of the surroundings — wasted. A lubricant keeps the surfaces apart so there is less friction and less waste. Say how, not just why.

sections.title: Key words: state what is meant by…

parts.title: The definitions
parts.html:
"State what is meant by" asks for the definition. Learn these as sentences.

TermWhat to write (mark-scheme form)Not this
Contact forceA force between objects that are touching (normal contact force, friction, tension, drag)."a push"
Non-contact forceA force that acts at a distance, through a field (gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic)."a force that does not touch"
FieldA region in which a mass / charge / magnetic material experiences a force."where the force is"
Normal contact forceThe force from a surface on an object pressing on it, at right angles to the surface.an unnamed "upward force" — "normal contact force", "(normal) reaction force" and "contact force" were all credited (Nov 2020 2H Q9(c)); name it and give its direction
FrictionThe force between two surfaces that opposes their relative motion."stickiness"
Interaction pairTwo forces, equal and opposite, of the same type, on different objects."balanced forces"
VectorA quantity with size and direction (force, velocity, displacement, acceleration, momentum)."a quantity with direction" alone
ScalarA quantity with size only (speed, distance, mass, energy, time)."a quantity with no size"
Resultant forceThe single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together."the total force" alone
EquilibriumThe state in which the resultant force is zero (and, for rotation, the moments balance): at rest or constant velocity."stationary"
Free body force diagramA diagram of one object showing all the forces acting on it as labelled arrows from its centre."a force diagram"
Moment of a forceThe turning effect of a force: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action, in N m."force × distance" with no 'perpendicular'
PivotThe point about which an object turns (hinge, fulcrum, axle)."the middle"
Principle of momentsIn equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a point = the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point."clockwise = anticlockwise"
LeverA rigid bar that turns about a pivot, transmitting and usually multiplying the turning effect of a force."a stick"
Effort and loadThe effort is the force applied to a machine; the load is the force it exerts on the object being moved.swapping them
GearA toothed wheel that transmits a turning effect to another by meshing; the moment on each is proportional to its radius."a cog that makes things go faster"
LubricantA substance (oil, grease) that separates sliding surfaces to reduce friction and the energy dissipated."something slippery"

questions.model: • The single force that would have the same effect as all the forces acting on the object.

questions.explain: "Sum of" and "in equilibrium" are both needed.

questions.text: State what is meant by a vector quantity and give one example. (1)
questions.model: • A quantity with size and direction, e.g. force / velocity / displacement / acceleration / momentum.

questions.text: State what is meant by a magnetic field. (1)
questions.model: • A region in which a magnetic material (or magnet, or current) experiences a force.

questions.text: State what is meant by equilibrium. (1)

The force between two surfaces that opposes their relative motion

sections.title: Finding a resultant by scale drawing
equations: \text{tip to tail; measure the closing line}

parts.title: The method
parts.html:
1. Choose a scale and write it down: "1 cm = 1 N" (or 1 cm = 10 N for big forces). Pick one that makes the drawing 5–10 cm across.
  2. Draw the first force as an arrow of the right length in the right direction, with a ruler.
  3. Draw the second force starting from the tip of the first (tip to tail), at its correct angle — use a protractor.
  4. The resultant is the arrow from the start of the first to the tip of the second. Measure its length and convert with the scale; measure its angle from a stated direction.

The parallelogram method gives the same answer: draw both forces from the same point, complete the parallelogram, and the diagonal from that point is the resultant. The June 2025 scheme (Q8(c)) accepted "a suitable parallelogram or triangle" for the direction mark; Nov 2020 (Q9(b)) accepted Pythagoras in place of the drawing. The marks were for the direction (judged by eye) and the size (within a tolerance — 2.5 to 3.5 for a 3 N answer in 2025, 48 to 52 N for 50 N in 2023), so the arrow must be drawn from the point the forces act on with an arrowhead (June 2023: "arrow head must be present"), labelled R, and within the tolerance. On the exam figure the two forces are already drawn from a point X: complete the parallelogram with plain construction lines (no arrowheads — June 2018 2H Q7(a)(ii): "reject answers which have any additional vectors drawn") and draw one arrow, R, from X along the diagonal.

Pythagoras check for forces at right angles: $R^2 = F_1^2 + F_2^2$; $3^2 + 4^2 = 25$, $R = 5$ N. If the drawing says 5.4, redraw. Trig is not required ("scale drawings only" in the spec) but is accepted if correct.

parts.title: Two ropes on a boat
parts.question: A boat is pulled by two ropes: 60 N due east and 80 N due north. Find the resultant force by scale drawing. (3 marks)
steps: Scale: 1 cm = 10 N. Draw 6.0 cm due east, then from its tip 8.0 cm due north.
Resultant: the line from the start to the tip measures 10.0 cm → 100 N.
Direction: the angle between the resultant and the east arrow measures 53° — 100 N at 53° north of east. Check: $60^2 + 80^2 = 10\,000 = 100^2$. ✓

questions.text: Forces of 5 N east and 12 N north act on an object. Calculate the size of the resultant (or find it by scale drawing).
Describe how to find the resultant of two forces at an angle using a scale drawing. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1ScaleChoose and state a scale (e.g. 1 cm = 1 N); draw the first force as an arrow of the correct length and direction.
2Tip to tailDraw the second force from the tip of the first, at the correct angle (protractor).
3MeasureDraw the resultant from the start of the first to the tip of the second; measure its length (convert with the scale) and its angle.

questions.text: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act at right angles. A student's scale drawing gives a resultant of 12 N. What should they conclude?
options: The drawing is wrong — Pythagoras gives 10 N
Resultants cannot be found for right angles
questions.explain: √(36 + 64) = 10 N. Always check a right angle with Pythagoras.

questions.text: A scale drawing uses 1 cm = 20 N. The resultant measures 6.5 cm. Calculate the resultant force.
Two 10 N forces act on a ring at 60° to each other. Explain, without a full drawing, why the resultant is less than 20 N but more than 10 N. (2)
questions.model:
• Force is a vector: the two forces are not in the same direction, so they do not add to the full 20 N.
  • At 60° apart they partly reinforce each other, so the tip-to-tail closing line is longer than either force alone — the resultant lies between 10 N and 20 N (it is about 17 N).

questions.text: In a scale drawing of two forces, where is the resultant drawn?
options: Between the tips of the two force arrows
From the start of the first force to the tip of the second
From the tip of the second back to the start
questions.explain: Start of the first to tip of the last in a tip-to-tail construction; on an exam figure, from the point the forces act on, along the parallelogram's diagonal.

checklist: Choose a scale and draw two forces tip to tail
Measure the resultant's size and direction
Check a right-angled case with Pythagoras
sections.blurb: Two forces at an angle do not add like numbers. Draw them to scale, tip to tail, and the resultant is the line from the start of the first to the tip of the second — measure its length and its angle. For a right angle, Pythagoras is the check.

sections.title: Resolving a force into two components
equations: \text{one force} \rightarrow \text{two at right angles with the same effect}

parts.title: Components by drawing
parts.html:
To resolve a force is to split it into two components at right angles — usually horizontal and vertical, or along and perpendicular to a slope — whose combined effect is the same as the original. The components are the two sides of the rectangle whose diagonal is the force.

  1. Draw the force to scale at its correct angle.
  2. From its tip, drop a perpendicular to each of the two directions you want.
  3. Measure the two sides from the start point: those are the components.

Why it matters: only the horizontal component of the rope's pull moves the sledge along; the vertical component just lightens it on the snow (reducing the normal contact force and so the friction). On a slope, the weight resolves into a component along the slope (which tends to make the object slide, and friction must match) and a component into the slope (which the normal contact force matches). The steeper the slope, the bigger the along-slope component.

Check with trig if you know it: the component along a direction at angle $\theta$ to the force is $F\cos\theta$; $10\cos 30° = 8.7$ N and $10\sin 30° = 5$ N. The spec asks for scale drawings only, so the drawing is what is marked.

parts.title: A sledge on the flat
parts.question: A child pulls a sledge with a 40 N force on a rope at 30° above the horizontal. (a) Find the horizontal and vertical components by scale drawing. (b) The friction on the sledge is 30 N. Calculate the resultant horizontal force. (4 marks)
steps: (a) Scale 1 cm = 5 N: draw 8.0 cm at 30° above horizontal. Drop perpendiculars: the horizontal side measures 6.9 cm → 35 N (34.6), the vertical side 4.0 cm → 20 N.
The horizontal component pulls the sledge along; the vertical component (20 N upwards) partly supports its weight.
(b) Horizontal resultant $= 34.6 - 30 = 4.6$ N forwards (about 5 N), so the sledge accelerates forwards gently.

questions.text: State what is meant by resolving a force. (1)
questions.model: • Splitting one force into two components at right angles to each other that together have the same effect as the original force.

questions.text: A 20 N force acts at 60° above the horizontal. A scale drawing (1 cm = 2 N) gives a horizontal side of 5.0 cm. State the horizontal component.
The same 20 N force at 60° above the horizontal: the vertical side of the drawing measures 8.7 cm. State the vertical component.
A box rests on a slope. Describe how to find the component of its weight acting along the slope, and explain why this component matters. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1DrawDraw the weight to scale, vertically downwards from the box's centre.
2PerpendicularsFrom its tip drop perpendiculars to the along-slope and into-slope directions; measure the along-slope side and convert with the scale.
3WhyThe along-slope component is the force tending to make the box slide down; friction must at least equal it for the box to stay at rest (the into-slope component is balanced by the normal contact force).

questions.text: A rope pulls a sledge at an angle above the horizontal. Which component moves the sledge along the ground?
questions.explain: Only the horizontal component acts along the direction of travel.

questions.text: As a slope is made steeper, the component of an object's weight along the slope…
questions.explain: At 0° it is zero; at 90° it is the whole weight.

sections.blurb: Resolving is adding in reverse: replacing one force at an angle with two forces at right angles that together have exactly the same effect. By scale drawing: draw the force, drop perpendiculars, measure.

sections.title: Equilibrium: three forces that close into a triangle

parts.title: Closing the triangle
parts.html:
Equilibrium means the resultant force is zero. Draw the forces tip to tail and the resultant is the line from the start to the finish — if that is zero, the finish is the start: the arrows form a closed shape. For three forces, a triangle.

To find an unknown: draw the known force(s) to scale; draw the directions of the unknown ones as lines from the right ends; where they meet closes the triangle; measure. Two tensions at known angles holding a known weight is the standard case.

The 'explain' version: for an object at rest the forces are balanced — in the vertical direction the upward components add up to the weight; in the horizontal direction the sideways components cancel. A picture hanging from two strings: each string's vertical component is half the weight; the horizontal components are equal and opposite. The wider the angle between the strings, the bigger the tensions needed for the same vertical component — which is why a washing line sags.

The spec's 'isolated object or system' (9.5): the triangle is drawn for the forces on one body (the knot, the sign, the box) — not mixing in forces on other things.

parts.title: A hanging sign
parts.question: A 10 N sign hangs from a knot held by two strings, each at 45° to the vertical. Use a scale drawing to find the tension in each string. (3 marks)
steps: Scale 1 cm = 1 N. Draw the weight: 10 cm straight down.
From the bottom draw a line at 45° to the vertical (the direction of $T_1$); from the top draw a line at 45° the other way ($T_2$). They meet, closing the triangle.
Measure: each side is 7.1 cm → 7.1 N. (Check: each vertical component is $7.1 \times \cos 45° = 5$ N; two of them hold the 10 N.)

questions.text: Explain why, for an object in equilibrium, the force vectors drawn tip to tail form a closed shape. (2)
questions.model:
• In equilibrium the resultant force is zero.
  • The resultant is the line from the start of the first vector to the tip of the last; if it is zero the tip of the last is back at the start — the shape closes.

questions.text: A 20 N lamp hangs from two identical chains at 30° to the vertical. Each chain's vertical component must be…
questions.explain: The two vertical components together support the 20 N.

questions.text: The lamp above: a scale drawing (1 cm = 2 N) of the closed triangle gives each chain tension as a side of 5.8 cm. State the tension.
A picture hangs from a single cord looped over a hook. Explain why the tension in the cord is greater when the cord is nearly horizontal than when it is nearly vertical. (2)
questions.model:
• The vertical components of the two parts of the cord must always add up to the picture's weight.
  • When the cord is nearly horizontal only a small fraction of each tension acts vertically, so the tension itself must be much larger to supply the same vertical component.

questions.text: A box rests on a rough slope. Name the three forces on it and explain how they can be in equilibrium. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1ForcesWeight (vertically down), normal contact force (at right angles to the slope), friction (up the slope).
2BalanceThe normal force balances the component of the weight into the slope; friction balances the component of the weight along the slope.
3TriangleDrawn tip to tail the three forces close into a triangle — the resultant is zero, so the box stays at rest.

questions.text: Three forces act on an object. Drawn tip to tail to scale, there is a gap of 2 cm (scale 1 cm = 5 N) between the tip of the last and the start of the first. What is the resultant?
questions.explain: The gap is the resultant: 2 cm × 5 N/cm = 10 N.

sections.title: Explaining motion from the resultant force

parts.title: The chain of reasoning
parts.html:
SituationForcesResultantMotion
skydiver just after jumpingweight large, air resistance smalldownwards, largeaccelerates downwards quickly
skydiver speeding upair resistance grows with speeddownwards, shrinkingstill accelerates, but less and less
terminal velocityair resistance equals weightzeroconstant velocity (not stopped)
parachute opensair resistance jumps to more than weightupwardsdecelerates (slows while still falling) until a new, lower terminal velocity
car at steady 30 m/sdriving force = drag + frictionzeroconstant velocity
driver presses the acceleratordriving force > resistive forcesforwardsaccelerates until drag has grown to match again
lift starting to go uptension > weightupwardsaccelerates upwards; at steady speed tension = weight again

The sentence pattern that scores: "[force A] is greater than [force B], so there is a resultant force [direction], so the object accelerates [direction]" — then, if the forces change with speed, "as the speed increases [force B] increases, the resultant decreases, until the forces are balanced and the velocity is constant". Four links; each is a mark.

Systems (9.5): a car towing a trailer is one system — the engine's driving force must overcome the drag and friction on both, and the tow-bar forces are internal. To find the tension in the tow bar, look at the trailer alone: tension − trailer's resistive forces = trailer's mass × acceleration.

parts.title: Parachute opens
parts.question: A skydiver is falling at terminal velocity when her parachute opens. Explain, in terms of the forces, what happens to her motion. (4 marks)
steps: At terminal velocity air resistance equals weight: resultant zero, constant velocity.
When the parachute opens the area increases, so air resistance increases and becomes greater than the weight.
There is now a resultant force upwards, so she decelerates — she slows down while still moving downwards (she does not move upwards).
As she slows, air resistance decreases until it equals the weight again: resultant zero, a new lower terminal velocity.

questions.text: A ball is dropped from a tall building. Explain why its acceleration decreases as it falls, and why it eventually falls at a constant speed. (4)
questions.model:
4 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1StartAt first only the weight is significant: resultant = weight, acceleration = g.
2Drag growsAs the speed increases, air resistance increases.
3Resultant shrinksResultant = weight − air resistance decreases, so the acceleration decreases ($F = ma$).
4TerminalWhen air resistance equals the weight the resultant is zero: no acceleration, constant (terminal) velocity.

questions.text: A car travels at constant velocity. The driver presses the brake. Which is true just after?
options: The resultant force is backwards and the car decelerates
questions.explain: Resistive forces now exceed the driving force.

questions.text: A car pulls a trailer. Explain why the tension in the tow bar is less than the driving force on the car. (2)
questions.model:
• The driving force has to overcome the resistive forces on the car and the trailer and accelerate both.
  • The tension only has to overcome the trailer's resistive forces and accelerate the trailer — a smaller job, so a smaller force.

questions.text: A lift of mass 500 kg hangs from a cable. ($g = 10$ N/kg)

parts.text: Calculate the tension in the cable when the lift moves upwards at constant velocity.
Calculate the tension when the lift accelerates upwards at 2 m/s².

questions.text: A cyclist stops pedalling on a flat road. Explain why she slows down and eventually stops. (2)
questions.model:
• With no driving force, the only horizontal forces are friction and air resistance, acting backwards.
  • The resultant force is backwards, so she decelerates; the resultant stays backwards until her velocity is zero.

questions.text: Which statement about an object at terminal velocity is correct?
options: Its weight is greater than the drag

questions.explain: Balanced forces, constant velocity.
