sections.title: Moments the hard way: angles, several forces, the beam's own weight
equations: \text{weight of a uniform beam acts at its centre}

parts.title: Four twists
parts.html:
1 — A force at an angle. Use the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action (extend the force's line and drop a perpendicular from the pivot), not the distance along the lever. It is always less than the lever length, so the moment is less than F × length (N6's diagram). If a question gives the angle, scale-draw the perpendicular distance or use the component of the force at right angles to the lever.

2 — Several forces. Decide the turning sense of each force about the pivot, calculate each moment, add the clockwise ones and add the anticlockwise ones separately, then set the totals equal. The June 2022 report praised answers that "set out separate moment calculations for S and P, then summed them".

3 — The beam's own weight. A uniform beam's weight acts at its centre (its centre of mass). If the pivot is at the centre that weight has no moment and can be ignored; if the pivot is anywhere else, the weight is one more force at distance (centre − pivot). This is the usual reason a see-saw problem "doesn't balance".

4 — Tipping. A plank on two supports, or a crane, tips about the edge support when the moment of the load about that edge exceeds the moment of everything on the other side. At the point of tipping the other support carries no force — set its force to zero and apply the principle of moments about the edge. A crane's counterweight is placed to make its anticlockwise moment match the load's clockwise moment; a heavier load must be carried closer to the tower.

The pivot force (reaction) is not found from moments but from the forces: in equilibrium the upward forces equal the downward forces, so pivot force = total weight on the beam.

parts.title: A non-uniform load and the beam's weight
parts.question: A uniform plank of weight 100 N and length 4.0 m rests on a pivot 1.0 m from its left end. A 300 N box sits on the left end. Calculate the force F that must be applied downwards at the right end to balance the plank. (4 marks)
steps: Distances from the pivot: box 1.0 m (left); plank's weight at its centre, 2.0 m from the left end, so $2.0 - 1.0 = 1.0$ m (right); F at the right end, $4.0 - 1.0 = 3.0$ m (right).
Anticlockwise: $300 \times 1.0 = 300$ N m.
Clockwise: $100 \times 1.0 + F \times 3.0 = 100 + 3F$.
Equilibrium: $100 + 3F = 300$, so $3F = 200$, $F = 67$ N (66.7). The pivot then pushes up with $300 + 100 + 67 = 467$ N.

questions.text: A uniform beam of weight 60 N and length 3.0 m is pivoted 0.5 m from its left end. Calculate the downward force needed at the left end to keep it horizontal.
questions.hint: The beam's weight acts at 1.5 m from the left end: 1.0 m from the pivot.

questions.text: A metre rule is pivoted at its 50 cm mark. A 2 N weight hangs at 10 cm and a 3 N weight at 30 cm. A single weight W hangs at 80 cm.

parts.text: Calculate the total anticlockwise moment about the pivot, in N cm.
parts.hint: Distances from the pivot: 40 cm and 20 cm.

questions.text: A force of 40 N is applied to the end of a 0.5 m lever at 60° to the lever. The moment is…
options: less than 20 N m, because the perpendicular distance is less than 0.5 m
questions.explain: Perpendicular distance = 0.5 × sin 60° = 0.43 m, moment 17 N m.

questions.text: A plank rests on two supports, A at its left end and B 1.0 m from its right end. A person walks towards the right end. Explain why the plank tips when the person passes a certain point, and what is true about support A at that moment. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1Moments about BBeyond B the person's weight has a clockwise moment about B that increases as they move further out.
2TippingThe plank tips when that moment exceeds the anticlockwise moment of the plank's own weight (acting at its centre) about B.
3Support AAt the point of tipping the plank is just lifting off A, so the force from A is zero.

questions.text: A tower crane carries a 20 000 N load 15 m from the tower. Its counterweight is 5 m from the tower on the other side. Calculate the counterweight needed to balance the load (ignore the arm's weight).
A 500 N uniform beam is pivoted at its centre and balanced: a 200 N load sits 3 m to the left and a 300 N load 2 m to the right. Calculate the upward force from the pivot.
walkthrough: Check it balances: anticlockwise $200 \times 3 = 600$ N m, clockwise $300 \times 2 = 600$ N m — equal in size and opposite in sense, so in equilibrium (the June 2023 2H show-that, Q6(b)(i), gave a mark for the comparison).
In equilibrium the pivot supports everything: $500 + 200 + 300 = 1000$ N upwards.

checklist: Use the perpendicular distance when a force is not at right angles
Add up several moments on each side
Include the weight of a uniform beam at its centre
Work out when a plank or crane will tip
sections.blurb: The 3- and 4-mark moments questions add one twist: a force at an angle, more than one load a side, a beam that weighs something, a pivot not at the centre, or the question of when a plank tips. The method does not change — only the bookkeeping.

sections.title: Levers: force multipliers, distance multipliers, and the work done
equations: E \times s_E = L \times s_L\ \text{(work in = work out)}

parts.title: Two equations, one idea
parts.html:
LeverPivot between?Effort distance vs load distanceEffect
crowbar, see-saw, scissors, plierspivot between effort and loadeffort further outforce multiplier
wheelbarrow, nutcracker, bottle openerload between pivot and efforteffort further outforce multiplier
tweezers, fishing rod, your forearmeffort between pivot and loadeffort closer than loaddistance / speed multiplier: a small movement of the effort moves the load a long way, but the effort must be bigger than the load

Equation 1 (moments): at balance, $E \times d_E = L \times d_L$. Effort four times as far from the pivot as the load → effort a quarter of the load.

Equation 2 (work): when the lever turns, both ends move along arcs, and the distance each moves is proportional to its distance from the pivot. The effort end moves four times as far as the load end. Work done = force × distance moved, so work by the effort $= \frac{L}{4} \times 4s = L \times s =$ work done on the load. A lever multiplies force by dividing distance; it never multiplies work. (With friction, the work by the effort is a bit more than the work on the load — efficiency below 100 %.)

The June 2023 scheme (Q6(b)(ii), the forearm): the biceps is a distance multiplier — attached close to the elbow, it had to pull with 212 N to hold the forearm and a ball whose own moment about the elbow was only 4.8 N m; the scheme accepted either adding up the total moment or adding the extra force the ball needed to the force already there.

parts.title: A wheelbarrow
parts.question: A wheelbarrow carries a 600 N load whose weight acts 0.4 m from the wheel axle. The handles are 1.6 m from the axle. (a) Calculate the effort needed to lift the handles. (b) The handles are lifted 0.2 m. Calculate the distance the load rises and the work done by the effort and on the load. (4 marks)
steps: (a) Moments about the axle: $E \times 1.6 = 600 \times 0.4 = 240$, so $E = 150$ N — a quarter of the load.
(b) Distances moved are in the ratio of the distances from the pivot: the load rises $0.2 \times \dfrac{0.4}{1.6} = 0.05$ m.
Work by the effort $= 150 \times 0.2 = 30$ J; work on the load $= 600 \times 0.05 = 30$ J. The same: the lever quartered the force and quartered the distance.

questions.text: A bottle opener's pivot is 1.5 cm from the cap and the hand pushes 12 cm from the pivot with 20 N. Calculate the force on the cap.
In a pair of tweezers the effort is applied closer to the pivot than the load. Which is true?
options: The force on the object is bigger than the effort
The force on the object is smaller than the effort but it moves further
The force and distance are both multiplied
questions.explain: A distance multiplier: more movement, less force.

questions.text: A crowbar lets a person lift a 900 N rock with an effort of 150 N. Explain why the person does not get 'something for nothing'. (2)
questions.model:
• The effort end moves six times as far as the rock (distances moved are proportional to the distances from the pivot).
  • Work done = force × distance: $150 \times 6s = 900 \times s$ — the work done by the effort equals the work done on the rock (more, with friction); only the force is multiplied.

questions.text: A see-saw lever lifts a 400 N load that is 0.5 m from the pivot. The effort is applied 2.0 m from the pivot.

parts.text: The effort end moves down 0.8 m. Calculate how far the load rises.
parts.hint: Ratio of distances from the pivot: 0.5 : 2.0.

parts.text: Calculate the work done on the load.
walkthrough: $400 \times 0.2 = 80$ J (the same as $100 \times 0.8$ by the effort).

questions.text: The biceps muscle attaches to the forearm 4 cm from the elbow; a weight is held in the hand 36 cm from the elbow. Explain why the muscle force is much larger than the weight held. (2)
questions.model:
• Taking moments about the elbow, muscle force × 4 cm = weight × 36 cm, so the muscle force is nine times the weight.
  • The forearm is a distance multiplier: the hand moves nine times as far as the muscle shortens, at the cost of a larger force.

checklist: Classify a lever by where the pivot, effort and load are
Calculate effort or load from the two distances
Explain why a force multiplier is also a distance divider: the work done is the same
sections.blurb: A lever can make a force bigger or a movement bigger, never both at once: effort × its distance from the pivot = load × its distance, and effort × distance it moves = load × distance it moves. The second equation is the one students miss, and it is the key to the winch question.

sections.title: Gears, force and work: the hand-winch 6-marker

parts.title: The winch and how the question was marked
parts.html:
Following the force. The effort $E$ on the handle makes a moment about Y's axle of $E \times$ (length of handle). That moment is passed to gear Y, whose teeth push on gear X's teeth with a force $F_{\text{teeth}}$ such that $F_{\text{teeth}} \times r_Y = E \times L$. The same tooth force pushes on X at X's bigger radius, so the moment on X is $F_{\text{teeth}} \times r_X$ — bigger by the ratio $r_X / r_Y$. X and the drum turn together, and that moment must at least match the moment of the load on the drum, $W \times r_{\text{drum}}$. Put together: $$E = W \times \frac{r_{\text{drum}}}{L} \times \frac{r_Y}{r_X}$$ — a long handle, a small drum and a big X compared with Y all make the effort smaller.

Following the distance. One turn of the handle moves the effort $2\pi L$ and turns Y once; X turns $\frac{\text{teeth}_Y}{\text{teeth}_X}$ of a turn, and so does the drum, raising the load $\frac{\text{teeth}_Y}{\text{teeth}_X} \times 2\pi r_{\text{drum}}$. The effort moves much further than the load rises. Work done by the effort = work done on the load (ignoring friction), so $E \times s_{\text{effort}} = W \times h$, and the effort is smaller than the load by exactly the ratio of the distances. Both pictures give the same answer — the moment picture explains the force, the work picture explains why it is not something for nothing.

How it was marked. The mark scheme listed the sizes (length of bar, number of teeth / radius of each gear, radius of drum), the equations (moment, work done, gear ratio, efficiency), and the links between them: "moment of effort = effort × length of handle", "moment of load on drum = load × radius of drum", "work done by effort = force × distance moved by the end of the handle", "work done on load = load × distance raised". What separated the levels: writing an equation in its general form ("moment = force × distance") reached Level 2; writing it in the parts of the winch ("moment of the handle = effort × length of the handle") — or saying the same thing in words — got into Level 3. Any of the equations would do.

Equation (Level 2 if left like this)The same equation in the parts of the winch (Level 3)Said in words (also Level 3)
moment = force × perpendicular distancemoment of the handle = effort × length of the handlethe longer the handle, the smaller the effort needed for the same moment
moment = force × perpendicular distancemoment of the force of gear Y on gear X = tooth force × radius of Y (the scheme's line), and the moment that force gives gear X = the same tooth force × radius of Xthe bigger gear X is compared with Y, the more the moment is multiplied
moment = force × perpendicular distancemoment of the load on the drum = load × radius of the drumthe smaller the drum, the smaller the moment the load produces, so the smaller the effort
work done = force × distance movedwork done by the effort = effort × distance the end of the handle moves (2π × handle length per turn)a longer handle means the effort moves further each turn
work done = force × distance movedwork done on the load = load × height the load rises (2π × drum radius per turn of the drum)a smaller drum lifts the load less far per turn
gear ratio = turns of one ÷ turns of the otherturns of the handle for one turn of the drum = teeth on X ÷ teeth on Ythe more teeth X has compared with Y, the more turns of the handle per turn of the drum, so the further the effort moves for each metre the load rises
efficiency = useful energy out ÷ total energy inefficiency = work done on the load ÷ work done by the effortfriction in the gears and bearings means the effort does a little more work than the load gains

The three errors the examiners reported. (1) Confusing work done with moment — both are force × distance, but in a moment the distance is the perpendicular distance from the pivot (N m), in work it is the distance moved along the force (J); mixing them capped answers at Level 2. (2) Saying the force of gear Y on gear X is increased — the force between the teeth is the same on both (an interaction pair); it is the moment that is bigger on X, because X's radius is bigger. (3) Describing the sizes without their effect — "the handle is long and X is bigger than Y" is Level 1; every size must be followed by what changing it does to the effort.

parts.title: The numbers
parts.question: In the winch drawn above, the handle is 0.30 m long, gear Y has radius 0.05 m (8 teeth), gear X has radius 0.15 m (24 teeth), the drum has radius 0.05 m and the load weighs 600 N. Ignore friction. (a) Calculate the moment of the load on the drum. (b) Calculate the force between the gear teeth. (c) Calculate the effort. (d) Check the answer using work done for one turn of the handle.
steps: (a) Moment of the load on the drum $= W \times r_{\text{drum}} = 600 \times 0.05 = 30$ N m. Gear X must supply this.
(b) Moment on X = tooth force × radius of X: $F_{\text{teeth}} \times 0.15 = 30$, so $F_{\text{teeth}} = 200$ N.

(c) The same 200 N acts on Y at 0.05 m: moment on Y $= 200 \times 0.05 = 10$ N m. Moment of the handle = effort × length of handle: $E \times 0.30 = 10$, so $E = 33$ N (33.3) — an 18 times smaller force than the load ($6 \times 3$).

(d) One turn of the handle: the effort moves $2\pi \times 0.30 = 1.88$ m, work by the effort $= 33.3 \times 1.88 = 63$ J. Y turns once, X and the drum turn $8/24 = \tfrac13$ of a turn, the load rises $\tfrac13 \times 2\pi \times 0.05 = 0.105$ m, work on the load $= 600 \times 0.105 = 63$ J. ✓

parts.title: A Level 3 answer
parts.question: Using physics principles, explain how the sizes of the handle, the gears and the drum determine the effort needed to lift the load. (6 marks)
steps: Handle: the moment of the handle = effort × length of the handle. For the moment the winch needs, a longer handle means a smaller effort; in the work picture, a longer handle means the end of the handle moves further each turn, so for the same work done the effort is smaller.

Gears: the force between the teeth is the same on both gears, but moment on gear X = tooth force × radius of X, and moment on Y = tooth force × radius of Y; because X has the larger radius (more teeth) the moment is multiplied by the ratio of the radii.

Equally, the turns of the handle for one turn of the drum = teeth on X ÷ teeth on Y, so the more teeth X has compared with Y, the more turns of the handle — the effort moves further for each metre the load rises, and work done by the effort = effort × distance the handle end moves must equal work done on the load = load × height raised, so the effort is smaller.

Drum: the moment of the load on the drum = load × radius of the drum, so a smaller drum means a smaller moment to overcome and a smaller effort (but the load rises less per turn, so more turns are needed).

Overall: effort = load × (drum radius ÷ handle length) × (radius of Y ÷ radius of X): long handle, small drum, X much bigger than Y → small effort. The work done is not reduced — the effort just moves much further than the load.
Efficiency: friction in the gears and bearings means the work done by the effort is a little more than the work done on the load, so the real effort is slightly larger than calculated.

questions.text: Two answers: A — "moment = force × distance, so the handle should be long"; B — "the moment of the handle = effort × length of the handle, so for the same moment a longer handle needs a smaller effort". Which reaches Level 3 and why?
options: B — the equation is written in the parts of the winch and its effect on the effort is stated
Both — they say the same thing
questions.explain: The general equation is Level 2; the equation in the parts, with the effect, is Level 3.

questions.text: A student writes: "The large gear X increases the force from gear Y." Explain what is wrong and write a correct sentence. (2)
questions.model:
• The force between the teeth is the same on both gears (an interaction pair); a gear cannot increase a force on itself.
  • Correct: "the same tooth force acts at the larger radius of X, so the moment on X (tooth force × radius of X) is larger than the moment on Y."

questions.text: A winch has a handle 0.40 m long on the axle of a 10-tooth gear (radius 0.04 m), which drives a 40-tooth gear (radius 0.16 m) fixed to a drum of radius 0.08 m. The load is 800 N. Ignore friction.

parts.text: Calculate the moment of the load on the drum.
Calculate the force between the gear teeth.
parts.hint: Moment on the 40-tooth gear = tooth force × 0.16.

parts.text: Calculate the effort on the handle.
parts.hint: Moment on the 10-tooth gear = 400 × 0.04; handle moment = effort × 0.40.
walkthrough: Moment on the small gear $= 400 \times 0.04 = 16$ N m.

parts.text: Calculate how far the load rises for one turn of the handle.
parts.hint: The drum turns 10/40 of a turn; one turn lifts $2\pi \times 0.08$.

parts.text: Show that the work done by the effort in one turn equals the work done on the load. Give the work done by the effort.

questions.text: Explain, using work done, why the effort on a winch handle is much smaller than the load it lifts. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1DistancesIn one turn the effort moves 2π × the handle length, while the load rises only a fraction of 2π × the drum radius (the drum turns fewer times than the handle because of the gear ratio).
2Equal workWork done by the effort (effort × distance the handle end moves) = work done on the load (load × height raised), ignoring friction.
3ConclusionSince the effort's distance is much larger, the effort is smaller than the load in the same ratio.

questions.text: A student writes "work done = force × distance, so a longer handle means more moment". Why did the examiners cap this at Level 2?
options: It confuses work done with moment — the distance in a moment is the perpendicular distance from the pivot, not the distance moved
Work done is not on the specification
questions.explain: The first of the three reported errors.

questions.text: The drum of a winch is replaced by one with twice the radius. Explain the effect on (a) the effort needed and (b) the number of turns of the handle to lift the load 1 m. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1EffortThe moment of the load on the drum = load × radius of the drum doubles, so the moment needed at the handle doubles and the effort doubles.
2TurnsEach turn of the drum lifts the load 2π × radius, now twice as far, so half as many turns of the handle are needed.
3WorkTwice the force for half the distance: the work done by the effort is unchanged (= load × 1 m).

checklist: Follow the force through a winch: handle → small gear → large gear → drum → load
Write moment, work and gear-ratio equations in the names of the parts (Level 3), not just in general (Level 2)
Explain the effect of changing each size on the effort, in both the moment and the work pictures
Avoid the three errors the examiners listed
sections.blurb: June 2025 Paper 2H Q9(b) asked how the sizes of a winch's parts decide the effort needed to lift a load. Students found it very hard. The difference between Level 2 and Level 3 was not more physics — it was writing each equation in the names of the parts.

sections.title: Friction: explaining it, using it, reducing it

parts.title: What the marks are on
parts.html:
Direction: friction acts along the surfaces, opposite to the motion (or the attempted motion) of one surface over the other. On a car's driving wheels it acts forwards — the tyre pushes back on the road, the road pushes forwards on the tyre — which is how a car moves at all.

Size: larger with rougher surfaces and with a larger normal contact force pressing them together (a heavier box is harder to push); it does not depend on the area of contact at GCSE level. Air resistance grows with speed and with area.

Energy: work is done against friction, $W = F \times d$, and that energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surfaces and the air — dissipated. In a machine it is why efficiency is below 100 %. (The June 2023 report, Q9(a)(iii): asked for a reason other than friction for wasted work in a pulley, most students still wrote "heat" or "squeaky wheels", which are friction; lifting the rope and pulley themselves, or stretching the rope, were the credited answers.)

Reducing it: lubricate (oil separates the surfaces), use ball bearings or wheels (rolling instead of sliding), polish the surfaces, streamline for air resistance. Each is a method; "reduce friction" is not.

Wanting it: brakes, tyres on a wet road (tread channels water away), shoes, climbing holds, a nail in wood, striking a match. There the answer is to increase friction: rougher surface, larger normal force, drier contact.

parts.title: Three marks on a box
parts.question: A 30 N box is pushed across a floor at constant speed with a force of 12 N. (a) State the size and direction of the friction. (b) Explain what happens to the energy transferred by the push. (c) Suggest one way to reduce the force needed. (4 marks)
steps: (a) 12 N, backwards (opposite to the motion): constant speed means balanced horizontal forces.

(b) Work is done against friction ($12$ J for every metre); the energy goes to the thermal store of the box's base and the floor — they warm slightly — and spreads to the surroundings, so it is dissipated.
(c) Put it on a trolley with wheels (rolling friction is much smaller than sliding) or polish / wax the floor — a specific method.
Not: "reduce the friction" — that is the aim, not a method.

questions.text: A car's engine turns the wheels. Explain how friction makes the car move forwards. (2)
questions.model:
• The turning tyre pushes backwards on the road (friction between tyre and road).
  • By the interaction pair the road pushes forwards on the tyre with an equal force — this is the driving force on the car.

questions.text: A question asks for a reason, other than friction, why the work done by the effort on a pulley is more than the work done on the load. Which answer scores?
options: Work is done lifting the rope and the lower pulley block as well as the load
questions.explain: Squeaks and heat are friction; "energy is wasted" is the question restated.

questions.text: Explain why a bicycle slows down and stops when the rider stops pedalling, in terms of forces and energy. (3)
questions.model:
3 marks — one mark per row.

PointForWhat you need to write
1ForcesFriction (bearings, tyres on the road) and air resistance act against the motion; with no driving force the resultant is backwards.
2DecelerationA backward resultant force means the bicycle decelerates until its velocity is zero.
3EnergyThe bicycle's kinetic store is transferred, by work done against the resistive forces, to the thermal store of the parts and the air — dissipated.

questions.text: Which change increases the friction between a crate and the floor?
options: Adding more weight to the crate
questions.explain: A larger normal contact force → larger friction.

questions.text: Give two different methods of reducing the friction in a machine's moving parts, and explain how one of them works. (3)
questions.model:
• Method 1: lubricate with oil or grease. Method 2: use ball bearings (or wheels) so parts roll rather than slide.
  • Lubrication works because the oil forms a layer that separates the two surfaces…
  • …so they no longer rub directly and the frictional force (and the energy dissipated as heat) is smaller.

questions.text: Explain why car tyres have tread patterns rather than being smooth. (2)
questions.model:
• On a wet road the grooves channel water away from the contact between rubber and road.
  • This keeps the rubber in contact with the road, maintaining the friction needed for grip when braking and steering (a smooth tyre would slide on a film of water).

checklist: Describe the direction of friction and what decides its size
Explain the energy transfer when work is done against friction
Give methods, not reasons, for reducing friction — and say when friction is wanted
sections.blurb: Friction questions are marked on specifics: name the surfaces, say which way the force acts, say where the energy goes, and when asked for a way to reduce it, give a method.

facts.q: Name the three non-contact forces and their fields.
facts.a: Gravitational (gravitational field), electrostatic (electric field), magnetic (magnetic field).

facts.q: Name five contact forces.
facts.a: Normal contact force, friction, tension, drag (air / water resistance), upthrust.

facts.q: In which direction does the normal contact force act?
facts.a: At right angles (normal) to the surface, pushing away from it.

facts.q: What is a field, in one sentence?
facts.a: A region in which a mass / charge / magnetic material experiences a force.

facts.q: How should a force arrow be drawn on a surface?
facts.a: Touching the point where the force acts, at right angles (normal) to the surface — the 2023 and 2024 fluid-force schemes gave a mark for each.

facts.q: Four features of an interaction pair?
facts.a: Equal in size, opposite in direction, same type of force, acting on different objects.

facts.q: Are the weight of a book and the normal contact force from the table an interaction pair?
facts.a: No — both act on the book and they are different types. They are balanced forces. The pair to the weight is the book pulling the Earth up.

facts.q: How do you find the partner of a force?
facts.a: Swap the two objects: 'A pushes B' ↔ 'B pushes A', same size, opposite direction.

facts.q: Vector or scalar: force, speed, velocity, mass, displacement, energy, acceleration, time, momentum, distance?
facts.a: Vectors: force, velocity, displacement, acceleration, momentum. Scalars: speed, mass, energy, time, distance.

facts.q: What do the length and direction of a force arrow show?
facts.a: Length: the size of the force (to scale). Direction: the direction of the force.

facts.q: Why can two 6 N forces have a resultant anywhere from 0 to 12 N?
facts.a: Force is a vector: the resultant depends on the directions — same direction 12 N, opposite 0 N, at an angle in between.

facts.q: Five rules of a free body force diagram?
facts.a: One object only; every arrow from (or through) its centre; correct directions; labelled with name and size; lengths in proportion.

facts.q: Why are force arrows drawn from the centre of the object?
facts.a: A force drawn at an edge would make the object rotate; through the centre it only changes its motion. The 2025 examiners penalised edge arrows.

facts.q: Free body diagram of a car at constant velocity?
facts.a: Weight down = normal contact force up; driving force forwards = drag + friction backwards. Four arrows, two equal pairs.

facts.q: Free body diagram of a ball at the top of its flight (no air resistance)?
facts.a: One arrow: weight, downwards. Nothing pushes up once it has left the hand.

facts.q: What is a resultant force?
facts.a: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together.

facts.q: How do forces along a line combine?
facts.a: Same direction: add. Opposite directions: subtract; the resultant is in the direction of the larger.

facts.q: What does a zero resultant force mean for the motion?
facts.a: The velocity does not change: the object is at rest or moves at constant velocity (steady speed in a straight line).

facts.q: What does a non-zero resultant force do?
facts.a: Accelerates the object in the direction of the resultant: speeds up, slows down or changes direction ($F = m a$).

facts.q: Does 'balanced forces' mean 'stationary'?
facts.a: No. A skydiver at terminal velocity has balanced forces and is falling fast.

facts.q: Equation for the moment of a force, with unit?
facts.a: Moment = force × distance normal (perpendicular) to the direction of the force, from the pivot. Unit N m.

facts.q: Why must the distance in a moment be the perpendicular distance?
facts.a: Only the part of the force at right angles to the lever turns it; pushing along the lever towards the pivot has no turning effect.

facts.q: Two ways to increase a moment?
facts.a: Increase the force, or increase the perpendicular distance from the pivot (longer spanner, handle far from the hinge).

facts.q: Why is the moment unit N m and not J?
facts.a: In a moment the distance is across the force (from the pivot); in work it is along the force. Different quantities.

facts.q: The commonest moments calculation error?
facts.a: Not converting cm to m — a 30 cm spanner is 0.30 m.

facts.q: State the principle of moments (both marks).
facts.a: For an object in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a point = the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

facts.q: What working do examiners expect in a principle-of-moments question?
facts.a: Each moment calculated as force × distance, the totals set equal — not just ratios of forces and distances.

facts.q: From where are the distances in a moments question measured?
facts.a: From the pivot — not from the end of the beam.

facts.q: Why can a wheelbarrow lift a load with a small effort?
facts.a: The wheel is the pivot; the load is close to it, the handles far from it: effort × long distance = load × short distance.

facts.q: Lever equation at balance?
facts.a: Effort × distance of effort from pivot = load × distance of load from pivot.

facts.q: How do gears transmit a turning effect?
facts.a: Teeth mesh; the force between the teeth is the same on both wheels; the moment on each wheel = that force × its own radius.

facts.q: Small gear driving a large gear: effect?
facts.a: Larger moment on the large gear, but it turns fewer times (slower) — a force multiplier.

facts.q: Large gear driving a small gear: effect?
facts.a: Smaller moment on the small gear, but it turns more times (faster) — a speed multiplier.

facts.q: How are numbers of teeth and numbers of turns related?
facts.a: Turns are in inverse ratio to teeth: a 10-tooth gear turns twice for one turn of a 20-tooth gear.

facts.q: Which way do meshed gears turn?
facts.a: Opposite directions. (A chain or belt keeps two wheels turning the same way.)

facts.q: To double the speed of an output gear, what do you add?
facts.a: A gear with half as many teeth meshing with it (June 2024).

facts.q: Where does energy go when work is done against friction?
facts.a: To the thermal store of the surfaces and surroundings — dissipated, no longer useful.

facts.q: How does a lubricant reduce friction?
facts.a: It forms a layer that separates the sliding surfaces so they do not rub directly; the frictional force is smaller, less energy is dissipated.

facts.q: "Suggest a way to reduce friction" — what kind of answer scores?
facts.a: A method: oil the axles, use ball bearings, polish the surface. 'Reduce friction' alone is a reason, not a method, and scores nothing (2025).

facts.q: Where should friction not be reduced?
facts.a: Brakes, tyres, shoes, matches — anywhere grip is the point.

facts.q: Steps to find a resultant by scale drawing?
facts.a: State a scale; draw the first force; draw the second from its tip (tip to tail); draw the resultant from the start of the first to the tip of the second; measure length and angle.

facts.q: Resultant of 3 N and 4 N at right angles?
facts.a: 5 N (Pythagoras: $9 + 16 = 25$), at 53° to the 3 N.

facts.q: Resultant of 6 N and 8 N at right angles? And 5 N and 12 N?
What did the 2025 scheme mark in a resultant-by-drawing question?
facts.a: The direction (judged by eye) and the size (within a tolerance) — the arrow must be drawn and labelled.

facts.q: What does it mean to resolve a force?
facts.a: To split it into two components at right angles that together have the same effect as the original force.

facts.q: How do you resolve a force by scale drawing?
facts.a: Draw the force to scale at its angle; drop perpendiculars from its tip to the two directions; measure the two sides.

facts.q: Which component of an angled rope pull moves a sledge along the ground?
facts.a: The horizontal component. The vertical component only reduces the normal contact force.

facts.q: Components of weight on a slope?
facts.a: One along the slope (tends to make it slide; friction opposes) and one into the slope (balanced by the normal contact force). Steeper → bigger along-slope component.

facts.q: What do forces in equilibrium look like drawn tip to tail?
facts.a: A closed shape (a triangle for three forces): the resultant is zero, so the last tip returns to the start.

facts.q: A 10 N sign on two strings at 45° to the vertical: each tension?
facts.a: About 7.1 N (each vertical component is 5 N).

facts.q: Why does a nearly horizontal washing line have a large tension?
facts.a: Only a small fraction of each tension acts vertically, but the vertical components must still add up to the weight, so the tensions are large.

facts.q: The sentence pattern for 'explain the motion'?
facts.a: [Force A] is greater than [force B], so there is a resultant force [direction], so the object accelerates [direction]; as speed changes, [force B] changes until the forces balance and the velocity is constant.

facts.q: What happens when a parachute opens at terminal velocity?
facts.a: Air resistance becomes greater than weight → resultant upwards → decelerates (still falling) → air resistance falls until it equals weight → new lower terminal velocity.

facts.q: Tension in a lift cable: constant velocity vs accelerating upwards?
facts.a: Constant velocity: tension = weight. Accelerating upwards: tension = weight + m a (greater than weight).

facts.q: Where does the weight of a uniform beam act?
facts.a: At its centre (centre of mass). No moment if the pivot is at the centre; otherwise include it as a force.

facts.q: How do you handle several forces in a moments problem?
facts.a: Find the turning sense of each about the pivot, calculate each moment, add the clockwise ones and the anticlockwise ones separately, set the totals equal.

facts.q: At the moment a plank tips off a support, what is true?
facts.a: The force from the other support is zero; take moments about the edge support.

facts.q: How do you find the force at the pivot?
facts.a: From the forces, not the moments: in equilibrium, upward forces = downward forces, so pivot force = total weight on the beam.

facts.q: A lever multiplies force by…?
facts.a: …dividing distance: the effort moves further than the load in the same ratio, so work by the effort = work on the load (ignoring friction).

facts.q: Example of a distance multiplier lever?
facts.a: Tweezers, a fishing rod, the forearm: effort closer to the pivot than the load — more movement, bigger effort than load.

facts.q: Biceps holding a weight in the hand: why is the muscle force so large?
facts.a: The muscle attaches close to the elbow; muscle force × short distance = weight × long distance, so the force is many times the weight (212 N in June 2023).

facts.q: Level 2 vs Level 3 in the 2025 winch question?
facts.a: Level 2: the equation in general ('moment = force × distance'). Level 3: the equation in the parts ('moment of the handle = effort × length of handle') or the same in words, with its effect on the effort.

facts.q: Moment equation in the parts of a winch (three versions)?
facts.a: Moment of the handle = effort × length of handle; moment on gear X = tooth force × radius of X; moment of the load on the drum = load × radius of drum.

facts.q: Work equation in the parts of a winch?
facts.a: Work done by the effort = effort × distance the end of the handle moves; work done on the load = load × height the load rises; the two are equal ignoring friction.

facts.q: Why is the effort on a winch much smaller than the load?
facts.a: Moment picture: long handle, small drum and big X over small Y multiply the moment. Work picture: the effort moves much further than the load rises, so for equal work it is a smaller force.

facts.q: Three errors in the 2025 winch answers?
facts.a: Confusing work done with moment; saying gear Y's force on X is 'increased' (the tooth force is the same, the moment is bigger); describing sizes without their effect.

facts.q: What does the gear ratio tell you in a winch?
facts.a: How many turns of the handle for one turn of the drum (teeth on X ÷ teeth on Y) — so how much further the effort moves than the load rises.

facts.q: Effect of a bigger drum on a winch?
facts.a: Larger load moment (load × radius) so a larger effort — but fewer turns, since each turn lifts the load further. Work unchanged.

facts.q: In which direction does friction act?
facts.a: Along the surfaces, opposite to the (attempted) motion of one over the other. On a driving wheel it acts forwards on the car.

facts.q: What increases sliding friction?
facts.a: Rougher surfaces and a larger normal contact force; not the area of contact.

facts.q: Reasons other than friction for wasted work in a pulley?
facts.a: Lifting the rope and the pulley block themselves; stretching the rope (June 2023). 'Heat' and 'squeaks' are friction.

facts.q: Four methods of reducing friction?
facts.a: Lubricate; ball bearings or wheels (rolling); polish the surfaces; streamline (for drag).

facts.q: State what is meant by: contact force.
facts.a: A force between objects that are touching (normal contact force, friction, tension, drag).

facts.q: State what is meant by: non-contact force.
facts.a: A force that acts at a distance, through a field (gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic).

facts.q: State what is meant by: field.
facts.a: A region in which a mass / charge / magnetic material experiences a force.

facts.q: State what is meant by: normal contact force.
facts.a: The force from a surface on an object pressing on it, at right angles to the surface.

facts.q: State what is meant by: friction.
facts.a: The force between two surfaces that opposes their relative motion.

facts.q: State what is meant by: interaction pair.
facts.a: Two forces, equal and opposite, of the same type, on different objects.

facts.q: State what is meant by: vector.
facts.a: A quantity with size and direction (force, velocity, displacement, acceleration, momentum).

facts.q: State what is meant by: scalar.
facts.a: A quantity with size only (speed, distance, mass, energy, time).

facts.q: State what is meant by: resultant force.
facts.a: The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting together.

facts.q: State what is meant by: equilibrium.
facts.a: The state in which the resultant force is zero (and, for rotation, the moments balance): at rest or constant velocity.

facts.q: State what is meant by: free body force diagram.
facts.a: A diagram of one object showing all the forces acting on it as labelled arrows from its centre.

facts.q: State what is meant by: moment of a force.
facts.a: The turning effect of a force: force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to its line of action, in N m.

facts.q: State what is meant by: pivot.
facts.a: The point about which an object turns (hinge, fulcrum, axle).

facts.q: State what is meant by: principle of moments.
facts.a: In equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a point = the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that point.

facts.q: State what is meant by: lever.
facts.a: A rigid bar that turns about a pivot, transmitting and usually multiplying the turning effect of a force.

facts.q: State what is meant by: effort and load.
facts.a: The effort is the force applied to a machine; the load is the force it exerts on the object being moved.

facts.q: State what is meant by: gear.
facts.a: A toothed wheel that transmits a turning effect to another by meshing; the moment on each is proportional to its radius.

facts.q: State what is meant by: lubricant.
facts.a: A substance (oil, grease) that separates sliding surfaces to reduce friction and the energy dissipated.

types.name: Moment of a force
equations: moment of a force = force × distance normal to the direction of the force
types.method: The moment, or turning effect, of a force is force × perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force. Change the distance to metres so the moment is in N m. To find the force or the distance, divide the moment by the other one.
commonErrors: Leaving the distance in cm, which gives a moment 100 times too big
Using the mass instead of the weight when a mass is given
Writing the unit as N/m or J: the moment is in N m

worked.question: A force of 20 N is applied to the end of a lever, 0.5 m from the pivot and at right angles to it. Calculate the moment of the force.
steps: Known: F = 20 N, d = 0.5 m. Unknown: moment.
moment = force × distance
moment = 20 × 0.5
moment = 10 N m

practice.question: A mechanic pushes on the end of a spanner with a force of 50 N. The spanner is 0.3 m long and the force is at right angles to it. Calculate the moment about the nut.
practice.hint: Multiply the force by the perpendicular distance from the nut.
walkthrough: F = 50 N, d = 0.3 m, find the moment.

practice.question: A door handle is 0.75 m from the hinges. A person pushes the handle with a force of 8 N at right angles to the door. Calculate the moment about the hinges.
practice.hint: The hinges are the pivot; moment = force × distance from the hinges.
walkthrough: F = 8 N, d = 0.75 m, find the moment.

practice.question: A cyclist pushes down on a pedal with a force of 150 N. The pedal is 40 cm from the centre of the crank. Calculate the moment about the centre of the crank in N m.
practice.hint: Change 40 cm to metres before multiplying.

practice.question: A wheel nut on a van needs a moment of 36 N m to loosen it. The wheel brace is 0.9 m long. Calculate the force needed at the end of the brace, applied at right angles to it.
walkthrough: moment = 36 N m, d = 0.9 m, find F.
moment = F × d → F = moment / d

practice.question: A 2 kg mass hangs from a metre rule 25 cm from the pivot. Calculate the moment of the mass about the pivot in N m.
practice.hint: Find the weight with W = m × g first, change 25 cm to metres, then multiply.

practice.question: A 1.5 kg bag hangs from a horizontal shelf bracket and produces a moment of 3 N m about the wall. Calculate the distance of the bag from the wall in cm.
practice.hint: Find the weight with W = m × g, then distance = moment / force and change to cm.

types.name: The principle of moments
equations: sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments
types.method: When a see-saw or beam is balanced, the total clockwise moment about the pivot equals the total anticlockwise moment. Work out the moment you can (force × distance), set it equal to the unknown side, and divide to find the missing force or distance. If two forces act on one side, add their moments before equating.
commonErrors: Using a distance measured from the end of the beam rather than from the pivot
Forgetting one of the forces when two act on the same side

worked.question: A see-saw is balanced on a pivot at its centre. A child weighing 300 N sits 2 m from the pivot on the left. Calculate how far from the pivot a child weighing 400 N must sit on the right to balance it.
steps: Known: left side F = 300 N at d = 2 m; right side F = 400 N. Unknown: d on the right.
anticlockwise moment = clockwise moment

practice.question: A metre rule is balanced on a pivot at its centre. A 20 N weight hangs 0.3 m to the left of the pivot. A force F pulls down 0.6 m to the right of the pivot and the rule is balanced. Calculate F.
practice.hint: Set 20 × 0.3 equal to F × 0.6 and divide.

practice.question: A beam is balanced on a pivot. A 50 N load sits 0.4 m from the pivot on one side. An 80 N load balances it on the other side. Calculate the distance of the 80 N load from the pivot.

A mobile hangs from a thread tied to a light rod. A 6 N ornament hangs 25 cm from the thread on one side. Another ornament hangs 15 cm from the thread on the other side and the rod is level. Calculate the weight of the second ornament.
practice.hint: Both distances are in cm, so they cancel: 6 × 25 = F × 15.

practice.question: A 40 kg child sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a see-saw. Calculate how far from the pivot a 30 kg child must sit on the other side to balance it.
practice.hint: Change each mass to a weight with W = m × g, then equate the moments.

practice.question: A metre rule is pivoted at its centre. On the left, a 10 N weight hangs 0.2 m from the pivot and a 5 N weight hangs 0.6 m from the pivot. A single force F acting 0.5 m to the right of the pivot balances the rule. Calculate F.
practice.hint: Add the two anticlockwise moments first, then set the total equal to F × 0.5.

practice.question: A plank rests on a pivot. On the left of the pivot, a 300 N box sits 1 m away and a 200 N box sits 2 m away. A person weighing 350 N stands on the right so that the plank balances. Calculate how far from the pivot the person stands.
practice.hint: Total the left-hand moments, then divide by 350 N.
